t: Largest Merge Of Two Strings - Greedy Interleaving with Suffix Comparison
o: We must consume both strings completely, one front character at a time, so every valid merge has exactly n+m characters - the only freedom is *which* string to pull from at each step, and we want the lexicographically largest outcome. Walk through Example 1 (`word1 = "cabaa"`, `word2 = "bcaaa"`): "c" beats "b", so take c from word1; then both fronts show b/b, a tie that cannot be settled locally, but comparing the remaining suffixes "caaa" vs "abaa" shows word2's side is larger, so take b then c from word2 to reach "cbc"; next b (word1) beats a, and everything left is a's, finishing at "cbcabaaaaa". Example 2 (`"abcabc"`, `"abdcaba"` -> `"abdcabcabcaba"`) sharpens the lesson: after the forced prefix "abd", both strings offer a..., and only a deeper comparison of "abcabc" against "aba..." reveals that word1 must feed the next characters. Lengths up to 3000 kill anything exponential, but one suffix comparison per emitted character costs at most O(n+m), so an O((n+m)^2) greedy (about 36 million character comparisons worst case) fits comfortably.
k: When the two front characters differ, greedily take the larger one - a merge starting with a smaller character can never win.
On ties, compare the entire remaining suffixes and consume from the lexicographically larger one.
The output length is fixed at n+m, so building the answer character by character is safe; only the choice sequence matters.

a.n: Approach 1: Greedy with Direct Suffix Comparison
a.i: At each step the optimal move is to take the front character of whichever remaining suffix is larger: if word1[i:] > word2[j:], any merge that starts by consuming from word2 is dominated by one that takes from word1 first (an exchange argument), because the first differing position of the suffixes decides everything that follows. Comparing whole suffixes - not just the current characters - is precisely what resolves ties correctly. No extra data structures are needed.
s: Keep pointers i and j into word1 and word2, plus an output buffer.
While both words are non-empty, compare the suffixes word1[i:] and word2[j:].
Append the front character of the larger suffix and advance that pointer.
When one word empties, append the remainder of the other and return the buffer.
a.t: O((n + m)^2) time - up to n+m picks, and a pick may compare suffixes of length up to n+m; fast for n, m <= 3000.
a.sp: O(n + m) space for the result buffer (transient suffix copies add only constant-factor overhead).

a.n: Approach 2: Two-Pointer Greedy Without Substring Copies
a.i: Same greedy rule, implemented allocation-free: on ties, advance both pointers together until they disagree (or one string ends) instead of materializing substrings for comparison. If word1 runs dry during the scan, its remainder was merely an extension of the shared prefix, so word2's suffix wins, and vice versa. Worth showing when an interviewer pushes on the hidden cost of repeated substring construction.
s: Advance i and j together while word1[i] equals word2[j].
Take from word1 if it still has characters left in the scan and either word2 ended or word1's mismatch character is larger; otherwise take from word2.
Repeat while both words are non-empty, then append the leftover tails.
a.t: O((n + m)^2) time - identical worst case, since one decision may scan O(n+m) tied characters; avoids slice allocations.
a.sp: O(n + m) space for the result.

w: Lead with the greedy and defend the tie-breaking rule explicitly - that is where interviews probe. The naive 'take the bigger current character' fails on inputs like `word1 = "cg"`, `word2 = "ca"`: taking either c looks fine, but word1's suffix "cg" beats "ca", so word1 must supply the c, yielding "ccga" rather than "ccag". Other pitfalls: forgetting to flush the leftover tail, and assuming O(n+m) total is achievable with plain comparisons (true linear time needs suffix-array or Z-function machinery). Follow-ups worth naming: the smallest merge (same skeleton, flipped comparator), merging k strings, and LC 321 'Create Maximum Number', which stacks subsequence selection on top of this same suffix comparison.
